trap.title: The disease, not the gene
trap.body: Many clues describe the CFTR gene or its chloride channel, and some real questions ask for CFTR itself, so players mix up the gene and the disease. Two other famous recessive diseases are traps too: sickle-cell disease, which bends red blood cells, and Tay-Sachs disease, which harms nerve cells. “Fibrosis” alone is not enough, and pulmonary fibrosis is a different lung condition.
trap.fix: Listen for “this disease” versus “this gene” or “this protein.” Thick mucus, salty sweat, the pancreas, chromosome 7, and F508del mean cystic fibrosis. Red blood cells, hemoglobin, and malaria mean sickle-cell disease.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cystic fibrosis (accept CF; do not accept “CFTR”)

topics.name: Cnidarians
topics.kicker: Jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones · Animals with stinging cells
topics.dates: More than 10,000 species, mostly in the sea
topics.briefing: Cnidarians (the C is silent) are soft-bodied water animals, such as jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras, that catch food with stinging cells. Each stinging cell holds a tiny coiled harpoon that fires faster than almost anything else in nature. They have no brain, just a net of nerves, and many switch between two body shapes: an attached polyp, like a coral, and a swimming bell called a medusa.
topics.answerHtml: Cnidarians (accept Cnidaria; prompt on coelenterates; do not accept a single member such as “jellyfish”; do not accept “ctenophores”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1962, Osamu Shimomura [“oh-SAH-moo shee-moh-MOO-rah”] isolated green fluorescent protein from the crystal jelly _Aequorea victoria_ [“ee-KWOR-ee-uh vik-TOR-ee-uh”], a member of this phylum, and he later shared a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for that work. Members of this phylum have no brain, only a simple nerve net.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with stinging cells called cnidocytes, including jellyfish and corals.

tossups.p: In “The Adventure of the Lion’s Mane,” Sherlock Holmes discovers that the culprit behind a seaside mystery is a giant member of this phylum. Members of this phylum have just two true tissue layers, separated by a jelly-like layer called the mesoglea [“mez-oh-GLEE-uh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes jellyfish, sea anemones, and corals.

tossups.p: _Turritopsis dohrnii_ [“tur-ih-TOP-sis DOR-nee-eye”], nicknamed the “immortal jellyfish,” is a member of this phylum that can turn back from an adult medusa into a young polyp. Many members of this phylum begin life as a free-swimming larva called a planula [“PLAN-yoo-luh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of radially symmetric animals with stinging cells, including corals and sea anemones.

tossups.p: In the 1740s, Abraham Trembley [“trahm-BLAY”] cut apart small freshwater members of this phylum and watched each piece regrow into a whole animal. Those animals, named for a many-headed monster from Greek myth, also reproduce by budding.
tossups.r: Those animals are hydras. For 10 points, name this phylum that also includes jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones.

tossups.p: Members of one class in this phylum have 24 eyes, some with lenses, arranged in four clusters called rhopalia [“roh-PAY-lee-uh”]. That class, Cubozoa, includes the sea wasp, one of the most venomous animals on Earth.
tossups.r: That class is the box jellyfish. For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that also includes corals and sea anemones.

tossups.p: The Portuguese man o’ war belongs to this phylum, but it is actually a colony of many small, specialized animals called a siphonophore [“sy-FON-uh-for”], floating under a gas-filled sail. Most members of this phylum catch prey using stinging capsules called nematocysts, which fire harpoon-like threads.
tossups.r: Those capsules are found inside stinging cells. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes jellyfish and corals.

tossups.p: Reef-building members of this phylum get much of their food from algae called zooxanthellae [“zoh-uh-zan-THEL-ee”] living in their tissues. When the water gets too hot, those animals expel the algae and turn white, a process called bleaching.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with stinging cells, whose members include the corals that build coral reefs.

tossups.p: In 2020, scientists found that _Henneguya salminicola_, a tiny parasite of salmon from this phylum, has no mitochondrial genome, so it cannot use oxygen to make energy the way other animals do. That parasite belongs to a group called myxozoans [“mik-suh-ZOH-unz”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones.

tossups.p: In 2017, scientists found that the upside-down jellyfish _Cassiopea_ [“kass-ee-OH-pee-uh”] slips into a sleep-like state at night, even though members of this phylum have no brain. Instead, members of this phylum have a simple nerve net spread through the body.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of radially symmetric animals with stinging cells, including corals and sea anemones.

tossups.p: In a process called strobilation [“stroh-bih-LAY-shun”], polyps of some members of this phylum split into a stack of tiny baby medusae called ephyrae [“EF-ih-ree”]. Many members of this phylum alternate between those two forms, with polyps reproducing asexually and medusae reproducing sexually.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes true jellyfish, hydras, and corals.

tossups.p: This phylum’s class Anthozoa includes sea anemones and corals, which live only as polyps, while its class Scyphozoa [“sy-foh-ZOH-uh”] contains the true jellyfish. Other classes in this phylum include Hydrozoa, home of the freshwater hydra, and Cubozoa, the box jellyfish.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of radially symmetric animals that catch prey with stinging cells.

tossups.p: Members of this phylum have only two true tissue layers, an outer epidermis and an inner gastrodermis, with a jelly-like layer called the mesoglea [“mez-oh-GLEE-uh”] between them. Their gastrovascular cavity has just one opening, which serves as both mouth and anus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes jellyfish and sea anemones.

tossups.p: When a tiny trigger bristle is touched, a coiled thread shoots out of a capsule in one of the fastest movements in nature, injecting venom into prey. That capsule, called a nematocyst [“neh-MAT-oh-sist”], is the key weapon of this phylum.
tossups.r: Nematocysts sit inside stinging cells called cnidocytes, which give this phylum its name. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes jellyfish and corals.

tossups.p: Clownfish live safely among the tentacles of some members of this phylum, protected by a special coat of mucus. Other members of this phylum built the Great Barrier Reef, the largest structure made by living things.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of stinging animals that includes sea anemones, corals, and jellyfish.

tossups.p: Stalked jellyfish, which belong to the class Staurozoa [“stor-oh-ZOH-uh”] in this phylum, attach themselves to seaweed with a stalk instead of swimming freely. Comb jellies look similar to members of this phylum, but they belong to a separate phylum and catch food with sticky cells instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of animals with stinging cells that includes sea anemones, corals, and true jellyfish.

clues.t: Phylum of jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras
Catch prey with stinging cells called cnidocytes, which give the group its name (from a Greek word for “nettle”)
Radial symmetry: body parts arranged in a circle around a central mouth
Two body forms: an attached, tube-shaped polyp and a free-swimming, bell-shaped medusa
A gastrovascular cavity with just one opening, which serves as both mouth and anus
Each stinging cell holds a capsule called a nematocyst, which fires a coiled, harpoon-like thread
No brain: a simple nerve net spreads through the body
Only two true tissue layers, the epidermis and gastrodermis, with jelly-like mesoglea between them
Reef-building corals host algae called zooxanthellae; in water that is too hot, corals expel them and turn white (bleaching)
Small freshwater hydras reproduce by budding and can regrow from pieces
Clownfish live safely among sea anemone tentacles, protected by a coat of mucus
Classes include Anthozoa (corals and anemones), Scyphozoa (true jellyfish), Cubozoa (box jellyfish), and Hydrozoa
The Portuguese man o’ war is a floating colony called a siphonophore, not a single true jellyfish
Many alternate forms: polyps reproduce asexually, while medusae reproduce sexually
Osamu Shimomura found green fluorescent protein (GFP) in the crystal jelly _Aequorea victoria_ and shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
In the Sherlock Holmes story “The Adventure of the Lion’s Mane,” the culprit is a lion’s mane jellyfish, one of the largest known jellyfish
_Turritopsis dohrnii_, the “immortal jellyfish,” can turn back from an adult medusa into a young polyp
In the 1740s, Abraham Trembley showed that cut-up hydras regrow; the hydra is named for the many-headed monster of Greek myth
Box jellyfish (Cubozoa) have 24 eyes, some with lenses, in four clusters called rhopalia; the sea wasp is among the most venomous animals
Their free-swimming larva is a planula; in strobilation, some polyps split into tiny baby medusae called ephyrae
The tiny salmon parasite _Henneguya salminicola_, a myxozoan, was found in 2020 to have no mitochondrial genome
The upside-down jellyfish _Cassiopea_ slips into a sleep-like state at night even without a brain
Touching a tiny trigger bristle fires the nematocyst’s thread, one of the fastest movements in nature
Coral polyps built the Great Barrier Reef, the largest structure made by living things
Stalked jellyfish (Staurozoa) attach to seaweed with a stalk instead of swimming
Comb jellies (ctenophores) look similar but form a separate phylum and catch food with sticky cells instead of stinging cells

trap.title: Phylum, not jellyfish
trap.body: Many clues describe one famous member, like a box jellyfish’s eyes or a hydra regrowing, so players blurt “jellyfish” or “hydra,” but the question wants the whole phylum. Comb jellies (ctenophores) are the sneakiest trap: they look like jellyfish but form their own phylum, swim with rows of beating cilia, and have no stinging cells. “Coelenterates” is an older name for a group that also included comb jellies, so it earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for “this phylum” or “these animals” and answer “cnidarians” (the C is silent). Stinging cells, nematocysts, polyps and medusae, and corals mean cnidarians; rows of shimmering cilia called combs mean ctenophores.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cnidarians (accept Cnidaria; prompt on coelenterates; do not accept a single member such as “jellyfish”)

topics.name: E. coli
topics.kicker: Rod-shaped gut bacterium · Biology’s favorite lab organism
topics.briefing: E. coli, short for _Escherichia coli_, is a rod-shaped bacterium that lives by the billions in the intestines of people and other warm-blooded animals. Most kinds are harmless or even helpful, but a few strains can cause food poisoning, which is why food-safety rules call for cooking ground beef all the way through. Because it is easy to grow and can divide about every 20 minutes, it is one of the most-studied living things in science.
topics.answerHtml: E. coli (accept Escherichia coli; prompt on Escherichia or coliform bacteria; do not accept “Salmonella” or “Shigella”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1885, a German-Austrian pediatrician who was studying bacteria in infants discovered this organism, which was later renamed in his honor. This organism is Gram-negative, so it stains pink, not purple, in a Gram stain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterium that lives in the human gut and whose harmful strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: In 1988, Richard Lenski began growing twelve populations of this organism in a long-term experiment, and after tens of thousands of generations, cells in one of them evolved the ability to feed on citrate when oxygen is present. Samples frozen every 500 generations serve as that experiment’s “fossil record.”
tossups.r: This organism can divide about every 20 minutes. For 10 points, name this rod-shaped gut bacterium.

tossups.p: In 1958, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew this organism on food containing heavy nitrogen-15 and followed its DNA through new generations, showing that DNA copies itself semiconservatively. Their experiment separated the DNA by density in a spinning centrifuge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium, a favorite model organism that lives in the human intestine.

tossups.p: In 1946, Joshua Lederberg and Edward Tatum showed that strains of this organism could swap genes, a process now called bacterial conjugation. Cells of this organism that carry the F plasmid, or fertility factor, build a bridge called a pilus to pass DNA to other cells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gut bacterium, known by a short form of its Latin name, whose dangerous strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: The restriction enzyme EcoRI, which cuts DNA wherever it finds the sequence GAATTC, takes the first part of its name from this organism. Restriction enzymes like that one help this organism defend itself by chopping up the DNA of invading viruses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in human intestines and is a favorite of biology labs.

tossups.p: In 1973, Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen made some of the first recombinant DNA by putting a plasmid carrying foreign genes into this organism. Genetically engineered strains of this organism later produced human insulin, which in 1982 became the first approved drug made with recombinant DNA.
tossups.r: This organism’s harmful strains can cause food poisoning. For 10 points, name this common gut bacterium, a favorite model organism.

tossups.p: The genome of this organism’s laboratory strain K-12, about 4.6 million base pairs long, was published in 1997 by Frederick Blattner’s team. In the human gut, this organism helps make vitamin K.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in the intestines and whose dangerous strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: A 1993 outbreak traced to undercooked hamburgers from Jack in the Box restaurants, which sickened hundreds of people, led the United States to tighten its rules on ground beef. That outbreak was caused by a strain of this organism called O157:H7, which makes Shiga toxin.
tossups.r: Most strains of this organism are harmless. For 10 points, name this bacterium that lives in the human intestine.

tossups.p: Grown on EMB, or eosin methylene blue, agar, colonies of this organism show a shiny, metallic green sheen. Water is tested for this coliform bacterium as a sign of contamination by sewage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium found in the human gut, whose harmful strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase showed that DNA carries genetic information by tagging T2 phages, viruses that infect this organism, with radioactive phosphorus and sulfur. Another virus that infects this organism, lambda, can hide inside its DNA as a prophage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterium that lives in the human intestine and is a favorite model organism.

tossups.p: François Jacob and Jacques Monod [“moh-NOH”] worked out the lac operon, a set of genes for digesting the sugar lactose, by studying this organism. This organism swims with whiplike flagella in a pattern known as “run and tumble.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped gut bacterium whose dangerous strains can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: During World War I, Alfred Nissle isolated a strain of this organism from a soldier who stayed healthy during an outbreak of dysentery, and that strain, Nissle 1917, became a widely used probiotic. In the gut, this organism helps make vitamin K.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium whose harmful strains, such as O157:H7, can cause food poisoning.

tossups.p: _Shigella_ [“shih-GEL-uh”] bacteria, which cause dysentery, are so closely related to this organism that some scientists consider them strains of it. Like _Salmonella_, this organism is a Gram-negative member of the family Enterobacteriaceae [“en-ter-oh-bak-teer-ee-AY-see-ee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in human intestines and is a favorite lab organism.

tossups.p: This organism is a facultative anaerobe, meaning it can grow with or without oxygen, so it can live in the oxygen-poor large intestine. This organism is Gram-negative, with a thin cell wall wrapped in an outer membrane.
tossups.r: Its species name refers to the colon. For 10 points, name this rod-shaped bacterium that lives in the guts of warm-blooded animals and is a favorite of biology labs.

tossups.p: Arthur Kornberg discovered DNA polymerase I, the first known enzyme that builds DNA, by studying extracts of this organism in 1956. Genetically engineered strains of this organism were later used to produce human insulin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gut bacterium that divides about every 20 minutes in the lab and whose harmful strains cause food poisoning.

clues.t: A bacterium that lives in the intestines of humans and other warm-blooded animals
Most strains are harmless, but some cause food poisoning, often from undercooked ground beef or contaminated raw produce
Biology’s favorite model organism: easy to grow, and it can divide about every 20 minutes
A rod-shaped (bacillus) bacterium, known by a short form of its Latin name
Gram-negative: stains pink in a Gram stain, with a thin cell wall wrapped in an outer membrane
Discovered in 1885 by a German-Austrian pediatrician studying babies’ gut bacteria, and later renamed in his honor
The dangerous strain O157:H7 makes Shiga toxin, which can harm the kidneys
Jacob and Monod worked out the lac operon, genes for digesting the sugar lactose, in this bacterium
Water is tested for this coliform bacterium as a sign of sewage contamination
In the gut, it helps make vitamin K
Engineered strains made human insulin, approved in 1982 as the first drug made with recombinant DNA
Joshua Lederberg and Edward Tatum discovered bacterial conjugation in it in 1946; the F plasmid builds a bridge called a pilus
Swims with whiplike flagella in a “run and tumble” pattern
Richard Lenski began growing 12 populations in 1988; after tens of thousands of generations, one evolved the ability to feed on citrate when oxygen is present
Meselson and Stahl grew it on heavy nitrogen-15 (1958) to show that DNA copies itself semiconservatively
The restriction enzyme EcoRI, which cuts DNA at GAATTC, is named for it
Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen made recombinant DNA in it in 1973 by adding a plasmid carrying foreign genes
The genome of lab strain K-12, about 4.6 million base pairs, was published in 1997 by Frederick Blattner’s team
A 1993 O157:H7 outbreak traced to undercooked Jack in the Box hamburgers led to tighter U.S. rules on ground beef
On EMB (eosin methylene blue) agar, its colonies show a metallic green sheen
Hershey and Chase tagged T2 phages, viruses that infect it, to show in 1952 that DNA is the genetic material
Bacteriophage lambda can hide inside its DNA as a prophage
The probiotic strain Nissle 1917 came from a World War I soldier who stayed healthy during a dysentery outbreak
_Shigella_ bacteria are so closely related that some scientists consider them strains of it; both are in the family Enterobacteriaceae
A facultative anaerobe that can grow with or without oxygen; its species name refers to the colon, where it lives
Arthur Kornberg discovered DNA polymerase I, the first known DNA-building enzyme, in its extracts in 1956

trap.title: Not Salmonella
trap.body: E. coli and Salmonella are both rod-shaped, Gram-negative gut bacteria in the same family, and both are famous for food poisoning, so players mix them up. Shigella is even closer: it is so similar to E. coli that some scientists call it a kind of E. coli, but it is still named separately. “Coliform” is a bigger group that includes E. coli, so it earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Lab-history clues, such as Meselson and Stahl, Lederberg and Tatum, the lac operon, EcoRI, and Lenski’s experiment, point to E. coli, biology’s favorite model organism. Raw eggs, chicken, and typhoid fever point to Salmonella. Say “E. coli” or the full name, not just “coliform.”
trap.line: Real answer line: E. coli (accept Escherichia coli; prompt on Escherichia)

topics.name: Flowers
topics.kicker: Reproductive structures of angiosperms · Ripen into fruits and seeds
topics.dates: Appear in fossils from the Cretaceous Period
topics.briefing: A flower is the part of a flowering plant that makes seeds. Bright petals, sweet scents, and sugary nectar lure bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, and bats, which carry pollen from one flower to the next. Once pollen reaches the sticky tip of the pistil, the flower’s ovary can swell into a fruit with seeds inside, which is why apples, cherries, and pea pods all start out as flowers.
topics.answerHtml: Flowers (accept flower, blossoms, or blooms; prompt on angiosperms or flowering plants; do not accept “stamens” or “pistils”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Charles Darwin called the sudden appearance of plants with these structures in the fossil record an “abominable mystery.” Amborella [“am-buh-REL-uh”], a shrub that grows only on the Pacific island of New Caledonia, belongs to the oldest surviving branch of the plants that make them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these reproductive structures of angiosperms, which are made of sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils.

tossups.p: In the ABC model, worked out by studying Arabidopsis [“uh-RAB-ih-DOP-sis”] and snapdragons, three classes of genes decide which part grows in each of the four rings, or whorls, of these structures. Mutant plants missing the C-class genes grow extra petals where their stamens should be.
tossups.r: Bees visit them to drink sweet nectar. For 10 points, name these plant structures whose ovaries ripen into fruits.

tossups.p: Carl Linnaeus sorted plants into classes and orders by counting the male and female parts inside these structures. He also proposed planting a garden “clock” of different species whose versions of these structures open and close at different hours of the day.
tossups.r: Green sepals protect these structures while they are still buds. For 10 points, name these colorful plant parts that attract bees.

tossups.p: A Madagascar orchid’s version of these structures has a nectar spur nearly a foot long, so Charles Darwin predicted that a moth with an equally long tongue must feed there. That hawk moth was finally described in 1903, after Darwin’s death.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant structures that attract pollinators with sweet nectar and colorful petals.

tossups.p: Bees, which cannot see red, follow nectar guides, ultraviolet patterns on these structures that human eyes cannot see. Hummingbirds usually visit red, tube-shaped kinds of these structures, while bats and moths visit white, strongly scented kinds that open at night.
tossups.r: Their ovaries later become fruits. For 10 points, name these plant structures that use color and scent to attract pollinators.

tossups.p: When the outer and inner rings of these structures look alike, as in tulips and lilies, their parts are called tepals. In monocots such as lilies, the parts of these structures usually come in threes or multiples of three, while in eudicots they come in fours or fives.
tossups.r: Their stamens hold up pollen-making anthers on thin filaments. For 10 points, name these reproductive structures of angiosperms.

tossups.p: The parasitic plant Rafflesia arnoldii [“ruh-FLEE-zhuh ar-NOLD-ee-eye”] makes the largest single one of these structures, which can be about a meter across and smells like rotting meat to attract flies. The titan arum makes the world’s largest unbranched cluster of tiny ones, which can grow taller than a person.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant structures, which usually attract pollinators with petals and sweet nectar.

tossups.p: Saffron, the world’s most expensive spice by weight, is made of dried stigmas picked by hand from the crocus’s version of these structures. Broccoli heads, artichokes, and the spice called cloves are all unopened buds of these structures.
tossups.r: Many have bright petals that attract bees. For 10 points, name these plant structures whose ovaries ripen into fruits.

tossups.p: Inside these structures, one sperm cell joins an egg while a second sperm cell joins two polar nuclei, a process called double fertilization. The second fusion makes the endosperm, the food supply that feeds a young plant inside its seed.
tossups.r: Afterward, the ovary of one of these structures ripens into a fruit. For 10 points, name these reproductive parts of angiosperms.

tossups.p: Botanists call these structures “imperfect” when each one is only male or only female, as in corn, which carries its male ones in the tassel at the top of the stalk. Holly trees have male and female ones on separate plants, so only the female trees grow berries.
tossups.r: Ones that have both stamens and pistils are called “perfect.” For 10 points, name these reproductive structures of angiosperms.

tossups.p: In the 1630s, prices for tulip bulbs whose versions of these structures had rare, flame-like stripes soared and then crashed in the Dutch Republic, an episode called tulip mania. Those stripes were later traced to a virus spread by tiny insects called aphids.
tossups.r: Florists sell these colorful plant parts in bouquets. For 10 points, name these structures made of sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils.

tossups.p: The calyx and corolla of one of these structures together make up its perianth [“PAIR-ee-anth”], which sits on a swollen stem tip called the receptacle. In a cluster of these structures, each one is held up by its own small stalk called a pedicel.
tossups.r: The calyx is made of sepals, and the corolla is made of petals. For 10 points, name these plant structures.

tossups.p: Orchids and snapdragons have zygomorphic [“zy-goh-MOR-fik”] versions of these structures, which can be split into mirror-image halves in only one way, while roses and buttercups have radially symmetric, or actinomorphic, versions. Pea plants also have zygomorphic ones, with one large “banner” petal on top.
tossups.r: Sweet nectar inside these structures attracts bees and butterflies. For 10 points, name these reproductive structures of angiosperms.

tossups.p: In the aster family, which includes daisies and dandelions, what looks like one of these structures is really a head of many tiny ones called florets. A daisy’s white “petals” are actually ray florets, while its yellow center is packed with disk florets.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant structures that make seeds and often attract bees with nectar.

tossups.p: Short-day plants such as poinsettias and chrysanthemums only start making these structures when nights grow long enough. Plants that rely on the wind, such as grasses and oaks, make small, plain versions of these structures with no bright colors or scent.
tossups.r: In those plants, the wind carries pollen instead of bees. For 10 points, name these reproductive structures of angiosperms, whose petals often attract pollinators.

clues.t: The reproductive structures of angiosperms, where seeds are made
Four main parts: sepals, petals, stamens (male), and pistils or carpels (female)
Bright petals, sweet scents, and sugary nectar attract pollinators such as bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds
After fertilization, the ovary ripens into a fruit and the ovules inside become seeds
Pollen made by the stamens must reach the sticky stigma of a pistil
Green, leaf-like sepals protect the bud; all the sepals together form the calyx
All the petals together form the corolla; calyx plus corolla is the perianth, which sits on a swollen stem tip called the receptacle
A stamen is a pollen-making anther on a stalk called a filament; a pistil is a stigma, a style, and an ovary
Monocots have parts in threes or multiples of three; eudicots usually have parts in fours or fives
“Perfect” ones have both stamens and pistils; “imperfect” ones are only male or only female, like corn’s male ones in the tassel
Hummingbirds visit red, tube-shaped ones; bats and moths visit white, strongly scented ones that open at night
Bees cannot see red, but they follow ultraviolet patterns called nectar guides
Double fertilization: one sperm joins the egg, and the other joins two polar nuclei to form the endosperm
A cluster of them on one stem is an inflorescence; each one in a cluster sits on a small stalk called a pedicel
Ones pollinated by the wind, as on grasses and oaks, are small and plain, with no bright colors or scent
Charles Darwin called the sudden appearance in the fossil record of plants that make them an “abominable mystery”
Amborella, a shrub found only on New Caledonia, belongs to the oldest surviving branch of angiosperms
ABC model: three classes of genes set which part grows in each of four whorls; plants missing C-class genes grow petals instead of stamens
Carl Linnaeus sorted plants into classes and orders by counting their male and female parts; he proposed a garden “clock” of species opening at set hours
A Madagascar orchid with a nectar spur nearly a foot long led Darwin to predict a long-tongued hawk moth, described in 1903
When sepals and petals look alike, as in tulips and lilies, they are called tepals
Rafflesia arnoldii makes the largest single one (about a meter across, smelling of rotting meat); the titan arum makes the largest unbranched cluster
Broccoli heads, artichokes, and cloves are unopened buds; saffron is dried stigmas picked from crocuses
Zygomorphic ones (orchids, snapdragons, peas) split into mirror halves only one way; actinomorphic ones (roses, buttercups) are radially symmetric
In the aster family, one head is really many tiny florets: a daisy’s white “petals” are ray florets, and its center holds disk florets
Tulip mania (1630s, Dutch Republic): bulbs of striped ones soared in price, then crashed; the stripes came from an aphid-spread virus
Holly has male and female ones on separate plants, so only female trees grow berries
Short-day plants such as poinsettias and chrysanthemums make them only when nights grow long enough

trap.title: The whole, not a part
trap.body: Many clues for this answer describe one of its parts, like the stamens, the pistil, the petals, or the ovary, so a quick buzz can come out as the part instead of the whole structure. Stamen and Pollen are separate answer lines, and “angiosperms” names the group of plants that makes flowers, not the structures themselves, so it only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “These structures” with sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils means flowers. “This male part” with an anther and a filament means stamen, “this powder” means pollen, and “this group of plants” means angiosperms.
trap.line: Real answer line: Flowers (accept flower, blossoms, or blooms; prompt on angiosperms or flowering plants; do not accept “stamens” or “pistils”)

topics.name: Serotonin
topics.kicker: Chemical messenger made from tryptophan · Helps regulate mood and sleep
topics.briefing: Serotonin is a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to pass signals to one another, and it helps regulate mood, sleep, appetite, and digestion. The body builds it from tryptophan, an amino acid found in foods like eggs, cheese, and turkey. Surprisingly, most of the body’s serotonin is made in the gut rather than the brain, and at night a small gland in the brain turns some of it into melatonin, a hormone that helps control sleep.
topics.answerHtml: Serotonin (accept 5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT; prompt on monoamine or indoleamine; do not accept “melatonin,” “tryptophan,” or “dopamine”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1948, Maurice Rapport, Arda Green, and Irvine Page at the Cleveland Clinic named this substance after isolating it from blood serum, because it made blood vessels tighten, changing their “tone.” It is often grouped with dopamine and norepinephrine as a monoamine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, made from the amino acid tryptophan, that helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite.

tossups.p: In the 1930s, Italian scientist Vittorio Erspamer found a chemical in cells lining the gut that made smooth muscle contract, and he named it enteramine. In 1952, enteramine was shown to be the same chemical as this one, which had been found in blood.
tossups.r: Most of the body’s supply of it is made in the gut. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter that helps control mood, sleep, and digestion.

tossups.p: Betty Twarog [“TWAR-og”], who studied this chemical in the muscles of mussels, found it in the brains of mammals in 1953 while working with Irvine Page. In the brain, most of the nerve cells that make it sit in clusters in the brainstem called the raphe [“RAY-fee”] nuclei.
tossups.r: The pineal gland turns it into melatonin. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter made from tryptophan.

tossups.p: The slowest step in making this chemical adds a hydroxyl group to an amino acid, and a second enzyme then removes a carboxyl group to finish the job. This chemical’s two-ring indole [“IN-dohl”] structure comes from that amino acid.
tossups.r: That amino acid is tryptophan. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite.

tossups.p: Blood cell fragments called platelets soak up this chemical from the blood and release it at a wound, where it helps nearby blood vessels narrow. Platelets cannot make it themselves; they collect it after cells in the gut make it.
tossups.r: In the brain, it acts as a neurotransmitter. For 10 points, name this chemical messenger linked to mood and sleep.

tossups.p: At night, the pineal [“PIN-ee-ul”] gland adds an acetyl group to this chemical and then a methyl group, turning it into a hormone that helps control the body’s daily rhythm. Light hitting the eyes slows that conversion.
tossups.r: That hormone is melatonin. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, made from tryptophan, that helps regulate mood and sleep.

tossups.p: Fluoxetine [“floo-OK-suh-teen”], sold as Prozac, belongs to a class of antidepressant medicines that block a protein pump called a transporter, which normally carries this chemical back into the nerve cell that released it. Blocking that reuptake lets this chemical stay longer in the synapse.
tossups.r: Those medicines are called SSRIs. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter made from tryptophan.

tossups.p: The enzyme monoamine oxidase breaks this chemical down, and some of the earliest antidepressant medicines worked by blocking that enzyme. Unlike dopamine and norepinephrine, which are catecholamines, this chemical is an indoleamine [“IN-dohl-uh-meen”]. Its molecular formula is C10H12N2O.
tossups.r: It is made from the amino acid tryptophan. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite.

tossups.p: Bananas, pineapples, and walnuts contain this chemical, but eating them does not raise its level in the brain, because it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Instead, the brain makes its own supply from an amino acid that can cross that barrier.
tossups.r: That amino acid is tryptophan. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter linked to mood and sleep.

tossups.p: When desert locusts are crowded together, a surge of this chemical in their nervous systems helps switch them from shy, solitary insects into members of a swarm. In mussels, it relaxes “catch” muscles, which can stay tightly contracted for a long time while using little energy.
tossups.r: In people, it helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter made from tryptophan.

tossups.p: Michael Gershon, who studied this chemical in the gut, wrote the 1998 book _The Second Brain_ about the gut’s own nervous system. Enterochromaffin [“EN-tuh-roh-KROH-muh-fin”] cells in the lining of the intestines make most of the body’s supply of this chemical, which helps trigger the wavelike muscle contractions called peristalsis.
tossups.r: In the brain, it helps regulate mood and sleep. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter made from the amino acid tryptophan.

tossups.p: Scientists have found more than a dozen kinds of receptors for this chemical. All but one kind are G protein–coupled receptors, while the exception is an ion channel that opens when this chemical binds. Neurons that release it in the brain mostly start in the brainstem’s raphe nuclei.
tossups.r: SSRIs such as Prozac block its reuptake. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter made from tryptophan.

tossups.p: The tiny hollow hairs of stinging nettles inject this chemical into the skin along with histamine and acetylcholine, adding to the sting. Its name comes from the blood serum where it was first isolated and from its effect on the “tone” of blood vessels.
tossups.r: The pineal gland uses it to make melatonin. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite.

tossups.p: Brainstem neurons that release this chemical fire fastest when an animal is awake, slow down during deep sleep, and fall nearly silent during REM sleep, the stage linked to vivid dreams. Like dopamine and norepinephrine, this chemical is a monoamine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter, made from tryptophan, that the pineal gland turns into melatonin.

tossups.p: After a neuron releases this chemical into a synapse, a transporter protein pumps it back into the neuron in a process called reuptake. The amino acid it is made from is often wrongly blamed for making people sleepy after a big turkey dinner.
tossups.r: That amino acid is tryptophan. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite.

Made from the amino acid tryptophan
Helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite
The pineal gland turns it into melatonin, a hormone that helps control sleep
SSRI antidepressants, such as fluoxetine (sold as Prozac), block its reuptake
Most of the body’s supply is made in the gut, by enterochromaffin cells in the intestinal lining
In the gut, it helps trigger peristalsis, the wavelike muscle contractions that push food along
Platelets soak it up from the blood and release it at wounds, helping blood vessels narrow
Most brain neurons that make it sit in clusters in the brainstem called the raphe nuclei
After it is released into a synapse, a transporter protein pumps it back into the neuron (reuptake)
A monoamine like dopamine and norepinephrine, but an indoleamine rather than a catecholamine
Broken down by the enzyme monoamine oxidase; some of the earliest antidepressants blocked that enzyme
Cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so the brain makes its own; bananas, pineapples, and walnuts contain it
The amino acid it is made from is often wrongly blamed for sleepiness after a turkey dinner
Named in 1948 by Maurice Rapport, Arda Green, and Irvine Page, who isolated it from blood serum; it affects the “tone” of blood vessels
In the 1930s, Vittorio Erspamer found it in gut cells and called it enteramine; the two were shown to be the same in 1952
Betty Twarog, who studied it in mussel muscles, found it in mammal brains in 1953 while working with Irvine Page
Tryptophan hydroxylase adds a hydroxyl group in the slowest step of making it; a second enzyme then removes a carboxyl group
Built around a two-ring indole structure; its molecular formula is C10H12N2O
At night the pineal gland adds an acetyl group and then a methyl group to make melatonin; light slows this
A surge of it in crowded desert locusts helps switch them from solitary insects to swarming ones
Relaxes the “catch” muscles of mussels, which can stay contracted for a long time using little energy
Michael Gershon, who studied it in the gut, wrote _The Second Brain_ (1998) about the gut’s own nervous system
Has more than a dozen kinds of receptors; all but one are G protein–coupled, and the exception is an ion channel
Stinging nettle hairs inject it into the skin along with histamine and acetylcholine
Brainstem neurons that release it fire most when awake, slow down in deep sleep, and nearly stop during REM sleep

trap.title: Not its chemical relatives
trap.body: Several separate answer lines share clues with serotonin. Tryptophan is the amino acid it is made from, and melatonin is the sleep hormone the pineal gland makes from it. Dopamine and norepinephrine are fellow monoamine messengers, but they are catecholamines made from a different amino acid, tyrosine, so naming any of these loses the tossup.
trap.fix: An indole ring, the raphe nuclei, platelets, the gut, enteramine, or SSRIs such as Prozac all point to serotonin. If the question asks what the pineal gland releases into the blood at night, say melatonin; reward, motivation, and L-dopa point to dopamine.
trap.line: Real answer line: Serotonin (accept 5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT; prompt on monoamine or indoleamine; do not accept “melatonin,” “tryptophan,” or “dopamine”)

topics.name: Vitamin C
topics.kicker: Vitamin found in citrus fruits · A lack of it causes scurvy
topics.dates: Identified in 1932; two Nobel Prizes in 1937
topics.briefing: For centuries, sailors on long voyages came down with scurvy: their gums bled, bruises appeared, and wounds healed slowly. The cure turned out to be vitamin C, found in citrus fruits, strawberries, peppers, and broccoli. Our bodies need it to build collagen, the protein that holds skin, blood vessels, and gums together, but unlike most other mammals, humans cannot make their own and must get it from food.
topics.answerHtml: Vitamin C (accept ascorbic acid or ascorbate; accept C after “this vitamin”; prompt on vitamin; do not accept other vitamins)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1747, the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind gave six pairs of sick sailors aboard HMS _Salisbury_ different treatments, such as cider, vinegar, and seawater, in one of the first controlled medical experiments. The pair given oranges and lemons recovered fastest because of this nutrient.
tossups.r: A lack of it causes scurvy, which makes gums bleed. For 10 points, name this vitamin found in citrus fruits.

tossups.p: Albert Szent-Györgyi [“SENT JUR-jee”] first isolated this substance from adrenal glands, calling it hexuronic acid, and later extracted large amounts of it from Hungarian paprika peppers. He won the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine partly for his work on it.
tossups.r: Sailors who lacked it got scurvy. For 10 points, name this vitamin found in oranges and lemons.

tossups.p: British chemist Norman Haworth worked out the ring-shaped structure of this compound and shared the 1937 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for that work. Tadeus Reichstein [“RIKE-shtine”] developed a method for mass-producing it from glucose in 1933.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vitamin whose lack causes scurvy, a disease that once struck sailors on long voyages.

tossups.p: In 1907, Norwegian scientists Axel Holst and Theodor Frølich discovered that guinea pigs fed a diet of grain and bread fell ill without this nutrient. Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make it, because their gene for the last enzyme needed to build it is broken.
tossups.r: Most other mammals make their own. For 10 points, name this vitamin, found in citrus fruits, whose lack causes scurvy.

tossups.p: Enzymes that add hydroxyl groups to the amino acids proline and lysine need this nutrient as a helper, so the body uses it to build strong collagen fibers. It also helps the intestines absorb iron from plant foods such as beans and lentils.
tossups.r: Without it, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly in a disease called scurvy. For 10 points, name this vitamin.

tossups.p: In the winter of 1535 to 1536, Iroquoian people near what is now Quebec City showed Jacques Cartier’s sick crew how to make a tea from the bark and needles of an evergreen tree, which supplied this nutrient.
tossups.r: Without it, sailors developed scurvy. For 10 points, name this vitamin found in citrus fruits.

tossups.p: During World War II, British volunteers gathered wild rose hips to make a syrup rich in this nutrient. Captain James Cook fed his crews sauerkraut to prevent a disease caused by a lack of it.
tossups.r: Lime juice given to British sailors for the same reason earned them the nickname “limeys.” For 10 points, name this vitamin found in citrus fruits.

tossups.p: Drops of fruit juice turn the blue dye DCPIP colorless when they contain this nutrient, a strong reducing agent. Food makers add this antioxidant, listed as E300, to keep cut fruit from turning brown.
tossups.r: It is found in oranges, strawberries, and broccoli. For 10 points, name this vitamin that prevents scurvy.

tossups.p: Two-time Nobel Prize winner Linus Pauling wrote a 1970 bestseller promoting large doses of this nutrient against the common cold. It dissolves in water rather than fat, so the body cannot store much of it, and extra amounts leave in urine.
tossups.r: Oranges and lemons are rich in it. For 10 points, name this vitamin whose lack causes scurvy.

tossups.p: Gram for gram, red bell peppers contain more of this nutrient than oranges do, and the Kakadu plum of Australia is one of the richest known sources of it. Cooking and long storage destroy much of it, because heat and air break it down.
tossups.r: A lack of it causes scurvy, which once killed many sailors. For 10 points, name this vitamin.

tossups.p: Although its chemical name calls it an acid, this compound has no carboxyl group; instead, a hydroxyl group on its five-membered lactone ring gives up a hydrogen ion. Its formula is C6H8O6, and most mammals make it from glucose.
tossups.r: Humans must get it from foods like oranges and broccoli. For 10 points, name this vitamin that prevents scurvy.

tossups.p: This compound’s chemical name, chosen by Albert Szent-Györgyi and Norman Haworth, comes from the Latin name of the disease it prevents, plus a prefix meaning “without.” Humans, other apes, monkeys, and some bats are among the few mammals that cannot make it.
tossups.r: Sailors who lacked it developed scurvy. For 10 points, name this vitamin found in citrus fruits.

tossups.p: In 1932, American chemist Charles Glen King reported isolating this nutrient from lemon juice, at about the same time Albert Szent-Györgyi identified it. Much earlier, Gilbert Blane persuaded Britain’s Royal Navy to give every sailor a daily ration of lemon juice, which supplied it.
tossups.r: Without it, sailors got scurvy. For 10 points, name this vitamin found in oranges, lemons, and limes.

tossups.p: In 1912, Casimir Funk suggested that a disease caused by a lack of this nutrient, along with beriberi and pellagra, came from missing substances he called “vitamines.” This nutrient helps the body build collagen, the protein that holds skin and gums together.
tossups.r: Strawberries and oranges are rich in it. For 10 points, name this vitamin whose lack causes scurvy.

tossups.p: This antioxidant dissolves in water and works alongside vitamin E, a fat-soluble antioxidant, by restoring vitamin E after it neutralizes harmful molecules called free radicals. Pet guinea pigs need extra amounts of it in their food, since they cannot make it.
tossups.r: Humans also need it from food, such as oranges. For 10 points, name this vitamin whose lack causes scurvy.

Found in citrus fruits like oranges, lemons, and limes, and also in strawberries, kiwifruit, and broccoli

In 1907, Axel Holst and Theodor Frølich found that guinea pigs fed grain and bread fall ill without it
Humans, other apes, monkeys, guinea pigs, and some bats cannot make it, because their gene for the last enzyme in the recipe is broken

During World War II, British volunteers gathered rose hips to make a syrup rich in it

Two-time Nobel winner Linus Pauling wrote a 1970 bestseller promoting large doses of it against the common cold

Charles Glen King isolated it from lemon juice in 1932; much earlier, Gilbert Blane got the Royal Navy to give sailors daily lemon juice

trap.title: Which vitamin?
trap.body: Several vitamins come with a famous deficiency disease, and a fast buzz can grab the wrong letter. A lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, a lack of vitamin D causes rickets, a lack of thiamine (vitamin B1) causes beriberi, and a lack of niacin (vitamin B3) causes pellagra. Vitamin K helps blood clot, and vitamin A helps with night vision.
trap.fix: Sailors, citrus fruits, limeys, collagen, James Lind, Szent-Györgyi, and paprika all mean vitamin C. Sunshine and rickets mean vitamin D. Saying just “vitamin” earns a prompt, so be ready to add the letter.
trap.line: Real answer line: Vitamin C (accept ascorbic acid or ascorbate; accept C after “this vitamin”; prompt on vitamin; do not accept other vitamins)

topics.name: Snakes
topics.kicker: Legless reptiles · Smell with forked tongues and swallow prey whole
topics.briefing: Snakes are legless reptiles found on every continent except Antarctica. They smell by flicking their forked tongues, have no eyelids or outer ears, and can stretch their jaws around prey wider than their own heads. Some, like cobras and vipers, use venom; others, like boas and pythons, squeeze their prey; and the reticulated python can grow more than 20 feet long.
topics.answerHtml: Snakes (accept snake, Serpentes, serpents, or ophidians; prompt on reptiles or squamates; do not accept “lizards”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: These animals collect scent particles from the air and ground and deliver them to a sensing structure in the roof of the mouth called the vomeronasal [“voh-muh-roh-NAY-zul”], or Jacobson’s, organ. The two tips of the body part that does the collecting help them follow scent trails.
tossups.r: That body part is a forked tongue. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles that include cobras, pythons, and vipers.

tossups.p: Some of these animals have heat-sensing holes between each eye and nostril, called loreal [“LOR-ee-ul”] pits, which let them detect the infrared glow of warm-blooded prey in total darkness. Others have smaller heat-sensing pits along their lips.
tossups.r: Pit vipers such as copperheads have the first kind, while boas and pythons have the second. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

tossups.p: Najash [“NAH-hahsh”], a fossil from Argentina named after the creature that tempted Eve in the Book of Genesis, shows that early members of this group still had hind legs. Some living members of this group keep tiny, claw-like spurs near the tail, the last traces of those legs.
tossups.r: Boas and pythons have those spurs. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles that smell with forked tongues.

tossups.p: Instead of eyelids, these animals have a clear scale called the brille [“BRILL-uh”], or spectacle, over each eye, which clouds over shortly before they shed. They have no outer ear openings, so they mostly sense sound as vibrations traveling through their jawbones.
tossups.r: They often shed their skin in one piece. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles, which include cobras and pythons.

tossups.p: The two halves of the lower jaw of one of these animals are not fused at the chin but joined by a stretchy ligament, so its mouth can open extremely wide. One African kind, the egg-eater, uses bony points on its neck vertebrae to crack eggs it has swallowed whole.
tossups.r: Cobras and pythons are examples. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles, which can swallow prey wider than their own heads.

tossups.p: Scientists long believed that members of this group that coil around and squeeze their prey kill it by suffocation, but a 2015 study showed that the squeezing mainly stops the prey’s blood flow. The longest member of this group is a reticulated species from Southeast Asia.
tossups.r: The heaviest is the green anaconda. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles, which also include cobras and vipers.

tossups.p: Members of this group in the family Elapidae [“ee-LAP-ih-dee”] have short front fangs fixed in place, while those in the family Viperidae [“vy-PAIR-ih-dee”] have long, hollow fangs that fold back when the mouth closes. The largest family in this group, Colubridae [“kuh-LOO-brih-dee”], includes many harmless species.
tossups.r: Elapids include cobras and mambas. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles that smell with forked tongues.

tossups.p: Fossils of Titanoboa, a member of this group that lived about 60 million years ago, not long after the dinosaurs died out, were found in a coal mine in Colombia. Scientists estimate it grew to about 40 feet long, making it one of the largest members of this group ever found.
tossups.r: Its closest living relatives include boas and anacondas, which squeeze their prey. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

tossups.p: After World War II, a brown, tree-climbing member of this group reached the Pacific island of Guam, probably hidden in military cargo, and wiped out most of the island’s native forest birds, which had never faced such a predator.
tossups.r: Burmese pythons have also invaded Florida’s Everglades. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

tossups.p: In tight tunnels, these animals bunch up and stretch out like an accordion, a method called concertina movement, while heavy members of this group creep in a straight line using their belly scales. The sidewinder moves sideways in loops that leave J-shaped tracks in the sand.
tossups.r: Most of the time, they slither in S-shaped waves. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

tossups.p: Members of this group molt in a process called ecdysis [“EK-dih-sis”], rubbing their snouts on rough surfaces to start peeling off the old outer layer. Each time certain American pit vipers molt, a new hollow keratin segment forms at the base of the warning rattle on the tail.
tossups.r: They often shed their skin in one piece, and pythons and cobras belong to this group. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

tossups.p: In most members of this group, the left lung is tiny or missing, leaving one long right lung to do most of the breathing. Their skeletons can contain hundreds of vertebrae, and almost every vertebra in front of the tail carries a pair of ribs.
tossups.r: Their long bodies have no legs at all. For 10 points, name these reptiles that include cobras, pythons, and vipers.

tossups.p: Harmless members of the genus Lampropeltis [“lamp-roh-PEL-tis”] copy the red, black, and yellow bands of venomous coral species in this group, an example of Batesian mimicry. The eastern hognose rolls onto its back and plays dead when threatened, sometimes letting its tongue hang out.
tossups.r: These animals smell by flicking forked tongues. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

tossups.p: To make antivenom for bites from these animals, scientists often inject horses with small doses of venom and then collect the antibodies the horses make. The inland taipan of Australia has the most toxic venom of any land-dwelling member of this group.
tossups.r: The king cobra is the longest venomous one. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

tossups.p: In Rudyard Kipling’s story “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi,” a mongoose battles two of these animals, Nag and Nagaina [“nah-GY-nuh”]. A staff with one of these animals wrapped around it, the Rod of Asclepius [“ass-KLEE-pee-us”], is a symbol of medicine.
tossups.r: Medusa had them instead of hair, and the infant Heracles strangled two of them. For 10 points, name these legless reptiles.

trap.title: Not every legless reptile
trap.body: Glass lizards and other legless lizards look almost exactly like snakes, worm lizards (amphisbaenians) are a separate group of burrowing reptiles, and caecilians are legless amphibians. Reptiles and squamates are bigger groups that include snakes and lizards, so those answers only earn a prompt.
trap.fix: Legless lizards have eyelids and ear openings and can drop their tails; snakes have neither eyelids nor outer ears. Forked tongues, Jacobson’s organ, heat pits, fangs, and swallowing prey whole all point to snakes, and “Serpentes” works too.
trap.line: Real answer line: Snakes (accept snake, Serpentes, serpents, or ophidians; prompt on reptiles or squamates; do not accept “lizards”)
